The Battle for the Marianas: The Mariana Islands Campaign of World War Two
It has always amazed me how the war in the pacific was mostly decided by luck during the battle of Midway.

The real downfall of the Japanese military during WWII was there lack of foresight in creating a larger training program for their carrier pilots. The program they had was too small to effectively provide sufficent replacements to make up for the lossess they suffered in the carrier engagements leading up to the Mariana's campaign. By the Battle of the Philippine Sea, virtually all of the original carrier pilot force had been killed off in combat during the preceeding four battles between Japanese and American aircraft carriers. After Philippine Sea, there were barely any Japanese Carrier pilots left of any ability. So few were left that most of the remaining Japanese carrier fleet was sacraficed as a decoy during the Battle of Cape Engano, with only 100 or so planes being launched by the Japanese carriers during the battle vrs some 600 by the Americans. Despite the lack of pilots, Japan still was building carriers right up to the end of the war, and it was the lack pilots that prevented the Japanese from maintaining their supply lines to the south east asian oil fields, since without air superiority on the trade lanes their tankers were shot to bits leaving them with no oil to fuel their battlefleet. So little fuel was left by the Battle of Okinawa that only a single battleship and a few smaller escorts were sent to challenge the Allied fleet, even though the Japanese still had at least 4 other battleships and several carriers left operational.
